questions.stem: The solution for the inequality \(\frac{3}{x-1}\lt 5\) can be expressed as:
questions.hint: Find x = 8/5 (equality) and x = 1 (undefined), then test each region or sketch.

steps.explain: Find where the two sides are equal and where the left side is undefined.
Sketch \(y=\frac{3}{x-1}\) and \(y=5\). The hyperbola is below the line for \(x\lt 1\) (where it is negative) and for \(x\gt\frac85\).
The inequality is strict and \(x=1\) is excluded, so both ends are open.
Multiplying both sides by \(x-1\) without care loses the \(x\lt 1\) part (options A, C).

keyPoints.note: Don't multiply by x − 1 (its sign is unknown). Use the critical values x = 1 and x = 8/5.

questions.stem: Solve \(\frac{4}{3x+1}\le1\)
questions.hint: Multiply by (3x + 1)² (always positive), factorise, and exclude x = −1/3.

steps.explain: \(x\neq-\frac13\). Multiply both sides by the square \((3x+1)^2\), which is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction.
Bring everything to one side and factorise.
Critical values \(x=-\frac13\) and \(x=1\); the parabola is positive outside them.
\(x=-\frac13\) makes the original undefined, so exclude it.

keyPoints.note: Multiply both sides by the square of the denominator so the sign doesn't flip.

questions.stem: Solve the inequality \(\frac{x^2-4}{x}\ge0\).
questions.hint: Critical values −2, 0, 2; test each interval; exclude x = 0.

steps.explain: Critical values: numerator zero at \(x=\pm2\); denominator zero at \(x=0\) (excluded).
Test a value in each interval.
Keep the intervals where the expression is \(\ge0\). Include \(x=\pm2\) (value 0) but not \(x=0\) (undefined).

keyPoints.note: Use the critical values x = ±2 and x = 0, then test signs.

questions.stem: Solve \(\dfrac{3}{2x+5}\le 1\).
questions.hint: Do NOT multiply by \(2x+5\) (it could be negative). Multiply by \((2x+5)^{2}\), which is always positive, so the inequality sign never flips. Remember \(x\ne-\dfrac{5}{2}\).

steps.explain: The denominator \(2x+5\) is zero at \(x=-\dfrac{5}{2}\), so \(x\ne -\dfrac{5}{2}\) (a vertical asymptote of the graph).
Multiply both sides by \((2x+5)^{2}\), which is positive for every allowed \(x\), so the \(\le\) sign stays the same. (One factor of \(2x+5\) cancels with the denominator.)
Move everything to one side and take out the common factor \((2x+5)\).
Simplify the bracket: \(3-2x-5=-2x-2\). Take out \(-2\) and flip the inequality when you divide by \(-2\) (negative).

Critical values: \(x=-\dfrac{5}{2}\) and \(x=-1\). A product of two linear factors is \(\ge 0\) OUTSIDE the roots (the upward parabola \(y=(2x+5)(x+1)\) is above the axis outside). Exclude \(x=-\dfrac{5}{2}\) because it is not allowed.

Check on the graph: the hyperbola \(y=\dfrac{3}{2x+5}\) is BELOW or on the line \(y=1\) for all \(x<-\dfrac{5}{2}\) (the branch is negative) and for \(x\ge -1\), where they meet at \((-1,1)\) (green). Test \(x=-2\): \(\dfrac{3}{1}=3>1\) ✗ (in between, so not a solution).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Multiply by the square of the denominator to avoid flipping signs; exclude the asymptote.

Why not the others: B is the solution of \(|2x-1|\le3\) (the middle); C forgets the left case; D has the wrong boundary \(x=1\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.hint: A fraction is \(\ge0\) when top and bottom have the SAME sign (or the top is 0). Use the critical points \(x=-2\) (top zero, allowed) and \(x=5\) (bottom zero, NOT allowed) and test each region.

steps.explain: Restriction: the denominator cannot be zero.

questions.stem: Solve \(\dfrac{3}{4x-1}\ge2\).
questions.hint: Never multiply an inequality by \(4x-1\) directly (it can be negative). Multiply by the SQUARE \((4x-1)^{2}\), which is always positive, or use a number line with the critical points \(x=\dfrac{1}{4}\) (undefined) and the solution of \(\dfrac{3}{4x-1}=2\).

steps.explain: Restriction: the denominator cannot be 0.
Multiply both sides by \((4x-1)^{2}\) (always positive, so the inequality sign stays).
Bring everything to one side and factorise \((4x-1)\).
A product \(\le0\) between its roots \(x=\dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(x=\dfrac{5}{8}\).
Remove \(x=\dfrac{1}{4}\) (undefined). Check with test points: \(x=0\): \(\dfrac{3}{-1}=-3\) ✗; \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\dfrac{3}{1}=3\ge2\) ✓; \(x=1\): \(\dfrac{3}{3}=1\) ✗.

questions.stem: Solve the inequality \(\dfrac{3}{x-1}\leq2\).
questions.hint: Never multiply an inequality by \((x-1)\) (its sign is unknown). Multiply by \((x-1)^{2}\) instead (it is always positive for \(x\neq1\)), move everything to one side, factorise and use a sign table. Exclude \(x=1\) at the end.

steps.explain: Exclude the value that makes the denominator zero: \(x\neq1\).
Multiply BOTH sides by \((x-1)^{2}>0\) (the inequality sign does not flip).
Expand the right side and collect everything on one side.
Critical points \(x=1\) and \(x=\dfrac{5}{2}\). The parabola \((2x-5)(x-1)\) opens UP, so it is \(\geq0\) OUTSIDE the roots: \(x\leq1\) or \(x\geq\dfrac{5}{2}\).
Remove \(x=1\) (division by zero). Check with test values (green = true, red = false): \(x=0\): \(\dfrac{3}{-1}=-3\leq2\) ✓; \(x=2\): \(\dfrac{3}{1}=3\leq2\) ✗; \(x=3\): \(\dfrac{3}{2}=1.5\leq2\) ✓.

Simplify the bracket: \(2x-6-x-2=x-8\).

questions.stem: The graph of the function \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}+1}{x}\) is shown. Sketch the graph of \(y=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f(x)}}\) showing all important features including turning point(s), intercept(s) and asymptote(s). Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: \(\sqrt{f(x)}\) exists only where \(f(x)>0\): for \(x>0\). Then \(y=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}}\) is a RECIPROCAL of a square root: the minimum of \(f\) at \(x=1\) (value 2) becomes a MAXIMUM of \(y\) with value \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), the vertical asymptote \(x=0\) becomes a point of the curve (\(y\to0\)), and large values of \(f\) give \(y\to0\) (the \(x\)-axis becomes an asymptote).

steps.explain: Domain: \(\sqrt{f(x)}\) needs \(f(x)\ge0\), and \(y=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}}\) needs \(f(x)>0\). From the graph (or \(\dfrac{x^{2}+1}{x}>0\)) this means \(x>0\): the whole left branch (\(x<0\)) is deleted.
Turning point: \(f'(x)=\dfrac{x\cdot2x-(x^{2}+1)}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}}=0\Rightarrow x=1\) (\(x>0\)). \(f(1)=2\) is the MINIMUM of \(f\). Reciprocal turns a minimum into a maximum.

As \(x\to0^{+}\): \(f\to\infty\), so \(y\to0\): the curve approaches the origin (open circle, since \(x=0\) is excluded). As \(x\to\infty\): \(f\to\infty\) so \(y\to0\): the \(x\)-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

There are no intercepts (the origin is excluded). The sketch is a hump starting at the open circle at the origin, with maximum \(\left(1,\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\), then falling towards the \(x\)-axis: graph A.
Why not the others: B is \(y=\sqrt{f(x)}\) (minimum \(\sqrt{2}\), asymptote \(x=0\)); C is \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) (includes \(x<0\)); D is symmetric in the \(y\)-axis (keeps \(x<0\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Reciprocal turns the minimum (1, 2) into a maximum (1, 1/√2); only x > 0 survives.

questions.stem: If \(f(x)=x^{2}-1\) sketch the graph of \(y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) indicating all intercepts and asymptotes. Which sketch is correct? (Red dashed lines are vertical asymptotes.)

steps.explain: \(f(x)=x^{2}-1=(x-1)(x+1)\) has zeros at \(x=\pm1\). Dividing by zero is impossible, so \(y=\dfrac{1}{x^{2}-1}\) has VERTICAL ASYMPTOTES \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\).
\(y\)-intercept: \(x=0\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{1}{-1}=-1\). \(x\)-intercepts: \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) is never 0, so there are none.

Signs: \(f<0\) between \(-1\) and 1, so the middle branch is NEGATIVE (\(\cap\)-shaped, maximum at \((0,-1)\)). \(f>0\) for \(|x|>1\), so the outer branches are POSITIVE and fall towards the \(x\)-axis: horizontal asymptote \(y=0\).
Why not the others: B is \(f(x)\) itself; C is \(\dfrac{1}{1-x^{2}}\) (signs flipped: the middle branch is above); D is \(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}+1}\) (no asymptotes).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the graph of \(y=f(x)\) where \(f(x)=x^{3}-3x\). Sketch \(y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) on the diagram, showing all turning points and asymptotes. Which diagram (A–D) is correct?
questions.hint: For \(y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\): (1) wherever \(f(x)=0\) (the \(x\)-intercepts \(-\sqrt3,0,\sqrt3\)) there is a VERTICAL ASYMPTOTE; (2) turning points stay at the SAME \(x\) but their \(y\)-value becomes the reciprocal (max \(\leftrightarrow\) min); (3) where \(f>0\) the graph is above the axis, where \(f<0\) below; (4) as \(|f|\to\infty\), \(\dfrac{1}{f}\to0\).

steps.explain: \(f(x)=x^{3}-3x=x(x^{2}-3)\) is zero at \(x=0,\pm\sqrt3\). Division by zero there gives three VERTICAL asymptotes (dashed).

Turning points: the same \(x\)-values. At \((-1,2)\) (a maximum of \(f\)) the reciprocal gives \(\left(-1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), a MINIMUM; at \((1,-2)\) (a minimum of \(f\)) we get \(\left(1,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), a MAXIMUM.
Sign of \(\dfrac{1}{f}\) equals the sign of \(f\): \(f<0\) for \(x<-\sqrt3\), \(f>0\) on \((-\sqrt3,0)\), \(f<0\) on \((0,\sqrt3)\), \(f>0\) for \(x>\sqrt3\).

Far from the origin \(f\to\pm\infty\), so \(\dfrac{1}{f}\to0\): the \(x\)-axis is a horizontal asymptote at both ends. Putting these together gives panel A: a U-shaped branch above the axis between \(-\sqrt3\) and \(0\) with minimum \(\left(-1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\); an upside-down branch below the axis between \(0\) and \(\sqrt3\) with maximum \(\left(1,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\); and two outer branches approaching the axis.

Why not the others: B has the turning points reflected (\(\left(-1,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\)) — it is the graph of \(-\dfrac{1}{f}\); C only has asymptotes at \(\pm\sqrt3\) and passes through the origin (but \(f(0)=0\) forces an asymptote at \(x=0\)); D has the wrong turning-point heights \((\pm1)\): they must be the reciprocals \(\pm\dfrac{1}{2}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

steps.explain: First graph: \(f\) crosses the \(x\)-axis at three single roots \(x=-2,0,1\) (green circles). Second graph: at each of the same three \(x\)-values it only TOUCHES the axis and bounces back up (a double root), and it never goes below the axis.

steps.explain: Test the idea \(y=\left(f(x)\right)^{2}\): a square is never negative, so the graph is entirely on or above the \(x\)-axis ✓. A single root of \(f\) becomes a double root of \(f^{2}\) (\((x-a)\to(x-a)^{2}\)), so the graph touches the axis ✓.

Where \(f\) is between 0 and 1 in size, squaring makes values smaller (the small bump near \(x=0.5\)); where \(|f|\) is bigger than 1, squaring makes it larger (the tall hump near \(x=-1.2\)). That matches the tall left hump and small right bump ✓.
Why not \(y=|f(x)|\) (option B)? That reflects the negative part up, so the graph would CROSS the axis at the roots with sharp corners (a V-shape), not touch it smoothly.

Why not \(y=\sqrt{f(x)}\) (A)? It only exists where \(f\ge 0\) (that is \(-2\le x\le 0\) and \(x\ge 1\)), so it would have NO graph for \(0<x<1\) or for \(x<-2\), but the second graph exists everywhere. Why not \(y=f(|x|)\) (C)? It is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, but the second graph is not.
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: How many solutions does the equation \(x^{\frac{1}{2}}=|x-1|-1\) have?
questions.hint: Draw \(y=x^{\frac{1}{2}}\) (that is \(\sqrt{x}\)) and \(y=|x-1|-1\) on the same axes. Each point where they meet is one solution.

steps.explain: Treat each side as a graph. \(y=x^{\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{x}\) starts at the origin and curves upward slowly (only for \(x\ge 0\)). \(y=|x-1|-1\) is the V-shaped graph \(y=|x|\) moved 1 right and 1 down, with vertex \((1,-1)\).
Find the \(y\)-intercept of the V: at \(x=0\), \(|0-1|-1=1-1=0\). So the V passes through the origin, which is also on \(y=\sqrt{x}\) (\(\sqrt{0}=0\)). That is solution 1: \((0,0)\).
For \(x\ge 1\), \(|x-1|=x-1\), so the right arm is \(y=x-2\). Solve \(\sqrt{x}=x-2\): square both sides (then check): \(x=x^{2}-4x+4\), so \(x^{2}-5x+4=0\), \((x-1)(x-4)=0\).
Check each in the ORIGINAL equation (squaring can add false solutions): \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{1}=1\) but \(1-2=-1\) ✗. \(x=4\): \(\sqrt{4}=2\) and \(4-2=2\) ✓.
For \(0<x<1\), the left arm is \(y=-x\) (negative) but \(\sqrt{x}>0\), so there is no intersection there. In total the curves meet at exactly 2 points: \((0,0)\) and \((4,2)\).
So the correct choice is option C.

steps.explain: Where is \(f\) negative? For \(x>1\) the factor \((1-x)\) is negative, so \(f<0\): the graph is below the axis for \(x>1\). Everywhere else \(f\ge 0\).
Absolute value rule: \(|f(x)|=f(x)\) where \(f\ge 0\) (no change) and \(|f(x)|=-f(x)\) where \(f<0\) (reflect in the \(x\)-axis). So only the part for \(x>1\) is flipped upward.

Result: the left part and the hump (max near \(x=0\), \(y=2\)) are unchanged; the curve goes down to \(x=1\) and now turns upward in a SHARP CORNER at \((1,0)\) and rises forever. All values are \(\ge 0\).

Compare the options: B is the original \(f\) (it goes below the axis); C is \(f(|x|)\) (symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, so it has a hump on both sides); D is \(f(x)^{2}\) (smooth touching at 1 instead of a corner). Only A is \(|f(x)|\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Consider the graph of \(y=f(x)\) shown below. Which of the following would have two MORE roots than \(f(x)\)?
questions.hint: Roots are the \(x\)-intercepts. \(f(x)\) is a cubic with a local maximum at about \(y=-1.6\) and a local minimum at about \(y=-4.4\), BOTH BELOW the \(x\)-axis, so it has only 1 root (at \(x=2\)). Ask what each transformation does to the number of times the curve crosses the \(x\)-axis.

steps.explain: Read the graph: one \(x\)-intercept at \(x=2\) (red point). The turning points are below the axis, so \(f(x)=0\) has exactly 1 root. We want a transformation with 3 roots.
A: \(y=-2f(x)\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis and stretches vertically. The \(x\)-intercepts do not move (zeros stay zeros), so still 1 root.

C: \(y=f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection in \(y=x\). The \(x\)-intercept of the inverse corresponds to the \(y\)-intercept of \(f\): the curve crosses the \(y\)-axis once (at \(y=-3\)), so it has 1 root, at \(x=-3\). D: \(f(x+3)\) is a shift 3 left; the roots just move (1 root).

B: \(y=f(x)+3\) shifts the graph UP 3. The local maximum \(\approx-1.6\) becomes \(\approx+1.4\) (above the axis) and the local minimum \(\approx-4.4\) becomes \(\approx-1.4\) (still below), so the curve now crosses the \(x\)-axis 3 times: two more roots.
Answer B: translating up by 3 gives 3 roots, which is 2 more than \(f(x)\).
So the correct choice is option B.

steps.explain: Where is \(f(x)\ge0\)? A square cannot be negative, so we need \(y^{2}=f(x)\ge0\). Reading the graph: \(f\ge0\) on the hump between the two left \(x\)-intercepts, and for \(x\) to the right of the third \(x\)-intercept.

questions.stem: Given the function \(f(x)=\dfrac{e^{2x}+1}{2e^{x}}\). Determine if the function is odd, even or neither by showing all of your working out. Which working is correct?

steps.explain: Replace \(x\) by \(-x\) in every place it appears (both in the numerator AND denominator).
Clear the negative powers: multiply the top and the bottom of the fraction by \(e^{2x}\) (the same number, so the value does not change).
Expand using index laws \(e^{-2x}e^{2x}=e^{0}=1\) and \(e^{-x}e^{2x}=e^{x}\).
Compare with the original: it is exactly \(f(x)\) (the numerator is \(e^{2x}+1\) in a different order).
\(f(-x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\), so \(f\) is EVEN: its graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis (e.g. \(f(1)=f(-1)=1.54\)). (Not odd: \(f(-x)\neq-f(x)\) because \(f(x)>0\).)

So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The diagram is a sketch of the graph of the function \(f(x)=-\dfrac{x}{x+1}\). Sketch the graph of \(y=(f(x))^{2}\), showing all the asymptotes and intercepts. Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: Squaring changes each height \(y\) to \(y^{2}\): all values become \(\geq0\); heights of 0 and 1 stay the same (\(0^{2}=0\), \(1^{2}=1\)); numbers between 0 and 1 get SMALLER; numbers bigger than 1 get BIGGER. Vertical asymptotes stay; the horizontal asymptote \(y=-1\) becomes \(y=(-1)^{2}=1\).

steps.explain: Intercepts: \(f(0)=0\), so \((f(0))^{2}=0\): the curve passes through the origin (and, since \(y\geq0\), it only TOUCHES the \(x\)-axis there).
Vertical asymptote: \(f\) has one at \(x=-1\); the squared function still blows up there, now to \(+\infty\) on BOTH sides (squares are positive).
Horizontal asymptote: as \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f(x)\to-1\), so \([f(x)]^{2}\to(-1)^{2}=1\). The new asymptote is \(y=1\).

Shape: for \(x>0\), \(f\) goes from 0 down toward \(-1\), so \(f^{2}\) rises from 0 up toward 1 (from below). For \(-1<x<0\), \(f>0\) falls from \(+\infty\) to 0, so \(f^{2}\) also falls from \(+\infty\) to 0. For \(x<-1\), \(f<-1\) (below the asymptote), so \(f^{2}>1\): comes DOWN from \(+\infty\) to approach \(y=1\) from above.
Compare: A matches all features. B is \(-[f(x)]^{2}\) (reflected: everything below the axis, asymptote \(y=-1\)); C is \(-f(x)\); D is \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) (asymptote at \(x=0\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Squares: ≥ 0, 0 and 1 unchanged, asymptote −1 → 1.

questions.stem: The diagram is a sketch of the graph of the function \(f(x)=-\dfrac{x}{x+1}\). Sketch the graph of \(y=x+f(x)\), showing all asymptotes and intercepts. Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: Add the two heights: \(y=x+\left(-\dfrac{x}{x+1}\right)\). Combine into ONE fraction first: \(y=\dfrac{x(x+1)-x}{x+1}=\dfrac{x^{2}}{x+1}\). Then divide to find the oblique asymptote.

steps.explain: Combine over the common denominator \(x+1\).
Vertical asymptote: denominator zero. The numerator is not zero there.
Oblique asymptote: divide \(x^{2}\) by \(x+1\) (long division): \(x^{2}=(x+1)(x-1)+1\).
Intercepts: \(y=0\Rightarrow x^{2}=0\): only \(x=0\) (a double root, so the curve TOUCHES the axis at the origin). \(y\)-intercept \(0\).

Turning points: \(y'=\dfrac{2x(x+1)-x^{2}}{(x+1)^{2}}=\dfrac{x^{2}+2x}{(x+1)^{2}}=0\Rightarrow x=0\) or \(x=-2\). At \(x=-2\): \(y=\dfrac{4}{-1}=-4\) (local MAX, curve left of the asymptote); at \(x=0\): \(y=0\) (local MIN).

Compare: A has asymptotes \(x=-1\), \(y=x-1\), the origin as a minimum and the maximum \((-2,-4)\). B is \(x-f(x)\) (asymptote \(y=x+1\)); C is \(-\dfrac{x^{2}}{x+1}\) (flipped); D has the vertical asymptote at \(x=0\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Combine: x + f = x²/(x+1); oblique asymptote y = x − 1.

questions.stem: The diagram is a sketch of the graph of the function \(f(x)=-\dfrac{x}{x+1}\). Solve the equation \((f(x))^{2}=f(x)\)
questions.hint: Do NOT divide both sides by \(f(x)\) (you would lose the solution \(f(x)=0\)). Bring everything to one side and FACTORISE: \(f^{2}-f=f(f-1)=0\). Solve each factor. Reject any answer that makes the denominator zero.

steps.explain: Move everything to the left side.
Factorise (common factor \(f(x)\)).
Case \(f(x)=0\): \(-\dfrac{x}{x+1}=0\) means the numerator is 0.
Case \(f(x)=1\): \(-\dfrac{x}{x+1}=1\). Multiply by \(x+1\) (\(x\neq-1\)).

Check both on the graph: the horizontal lines \(y=0\) (green) and \(y=1\) (orange) cut \(f\) at \(x=0\) and \(x=-\dfrac{1}{2}\) (red dots). Check by substitution: \(f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\dfrac{-0.5}{0.5}=1\) and \(1^{2}=1\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign in \(-2x=1\); C is the vertical asymptote (undefined); D forgets \(f=0\) (dividing by \(f\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: f² = f → f(f − 1) = 0; never divide by f.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the graph \(y=f(x)\) (a curve in the second quadrant coming down from the upper left and levelling off at the \(y\)-axis). Which diagram shows the graph \(y=f^{-1}(x)\)?
questions.hint: The graph of \(y=f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection of \(y=f(x)\) in the line \(y=x\): every point \((a,b)\) becomes \((b,a)\).

steps.explain: Reflecting in the line \(y=x\) swaps the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of every point. The curve starts at the top left and ends at the point \((0,c)\) on the positive \(y\)-axis where it is flat.
The end point \((0,c)\) with \(c>0\) becomes \((c,0)\): a point on the POSITIVE \(x\)-axis. That removes A and C (their ends are on the negative \(x\)-axis).
The flat (horizontal) tangent at \((0,c)\) becomes a VERTICAL tangent at \((c,0)\), so the inverse leaves the \(x\)-axis going straight up or down.

The original has \(x\le 0\) (negative \(x\)-values) and \(y\ge c\) (large positive \(y\)). So the inverse has \(y\le 0\) (negative \(y\)-values) and \(x\ge c\). Negative \(y\) means the graph is BELOW the \(x\)-axis, on the right: the fourth quadrant.

Only D starts on the positive \(x\)-axis with a vertical tangent and goes down to the right. B has the right start but goes UP (positive \(y\)), which would be the inverse of a graph in the fourth quadrant.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Reflect in y equals x: swap coordinates; domain and range swap, flat becomes vertical.

So the correct choice is option A.

steps.explain: Find the axis of symmetry of \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5\): \(x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}\).
The parabola is symmetric about \(x=2\), so two different \(x\)-values (such as \(x=1\) and \(x=3\)) give the same \(y\)-value: not one-to-one.

So the correct choice is option A.

So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\). Explain why the domain of \(f(x)\) is \(0\le x\le16\).
questions.hint: A square root needs a NON-NEGATIVE inside. There are TWO square roots, so two conditions: the INNER \(\sqrt{x}\) needs \(x\ge0\); the OUTER \(\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\) needs \(4-\sqrt{x}\ge0\). Combine them.

steps.explain: Inner root \(\sqrt{x}\) is defined only when \(x\ge0\).
Outer root \(\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\) needs \(4-\sqrt{x}\ge0\). Rearrange (add \(\sqrt{x}\) to both sides): \(\sqrt{x}\le4\).
Square both sides (both sides are non-negative so the inequality direction is kept): \(x\le16\).
Both conditions together.

Why not the others: B uses \(>0\) (the inside may equal 0, so \(x=16\) is allowed: \(f(16)=0\)); C reverses the inequality when moving \(-\sqrt{x}\); D squares incorrectly (\(\sqrt{x}\le4\) gives \(x\le16\), not \(x\le4\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\) has domain \(0\le x\le16\). Prove \(f(x)\) is a decreasing function and find its range.
questions.hint: A function is DECREASING when \(f'(x)<0\) throughout its domain. Differentiate with the chain rule (outer \(\sqrt{\ }\), inner \(4-x^{\frac{1}{2}}\)). A decreasing function takes its LARGEST value at the left end and SMALLEST at the right end of the domain: evaluate \(f(0)\) and \(f(16)\).

steps.explain: Rewrite with indices: \(f(x)=\left(4-x^{\frac12}\right)^{\frac12}\).
Chain rule: bring down \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), reduce the power by 1, multiply by the derivative of the inside \(-\dfrac12x^{-\frac12}\).
Sign: \(\sqrt{x}>0\) and \(\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}>0\) inside the domain (\(0<x<16\)), so the denominator is positive and the minus sign in front makes \(f'(x)<0\). Therefore \(f\) is DECREASING.
Range: a decreasing function's range lies between the values at the two endpoints: \(f(0)=\sqrt{4-0}=2\) and \(f(16)=\sqrt{4-4}=0\).

Why not the others: B takes the domain values (16) as the range; C has the wrong sign of the derivative (the inside \(4-\sqrt{x}\) decreases); D mis-evaluates the sign of \(f\) (a square root is never negative).
So the correct choice is option A.

A: \(\sin|x|\) is an EVEN function (not one-to-one on \([-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2]\)): \(\sin|{-1}|=\sin|1|\). No inverse function. ✗

C: \(|e^{x}|=e^{x}\): inverse \(\ln x\ne e^{x}\). ✗
So only \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\) is its own inverse (its graph is symmetric about \(y=x\)).
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: The function \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x+7\) has an inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\) in the domain \(x\ge2\). What is the value of \(f^{-1}(f(m))\), where \(m\) is a real number NOT in the domain \(x\ge2\)?
questions.hint: Complete the square to see the axis of symmetry \(x=2\). \(f^{-1}(f(m))\) gives \(m\) back ONLY when \(m\) is in the domain \(x\ge2\). Here \(m<2\), so you get the mirror image of \(m\) in the line \(x=2\).

steps.explain: Complete the square.
The parabola has vertex \((2,3)\) and axis of symmetry \(x=2\). The inverse exists only for the RIGHT half \(x\ge2\) (solid blue); \(m<2\) lies on the left half (dashed).

\(f(m)\) is a \(y\)-value. The inverse \(f^{-1}\) takes that \(y\)-value to the \(x\) on the RIGHT half with the same \(y\). The point on the right half with the same height as \(m\) is the mirror image of \(m\) in \(x=2\) (orange line).
The mirror image of \(m\) in \(x=2\) is \(2+(2-m)=4-m\) (as far to the right of 2 as \(m\) is to the left). And \(4-m>2\) because \(m<2\), so it is in the domain.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Mirror m in the axis of symmetry x = 2 to get 4 − m.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=(x-1)^{2}\), for the domain \(x>1\). Find any values of \(x\) for which \(f(x)=f^{-1}(x)\).
questions.hint: A function and its inverse are mirror images in the line \(y=x\), so they can only meet ON the line \(y=x\) (for an increasing function). Solve \(f(x)=x\), then check the domain.

steps.explain: \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) intersect where \(f(x)=x\) (on the line \(y=x\)).
Expand and collect.
Quadratic formula (\(a=1,\ b=-3,\ c=1\)).
Domain \(x>1\): \(\dfrac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx0.38\) is NOT allowed; \(\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx2.62>1\) is.

Check: \(\left(2.618-1\right)^{2}=2.618\) ✓. (The printed solution works with \(f(x)=2(x-1)^{2}\) and gets \(x=2\); for the function in the question, \(f(x)=(x-1)^{2}\), the answer is \(\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\).)
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: f equals its inverse on the line y = x: solve (x − 1) squared = x with x > 1.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5\). Find the point(s) of intersection of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=f^{-1}(x)\) in the domain determined in part (i).
questions.hint: A function and its inverse are reflections in the line \(y=x\), so they intersect where \(f(x)=x\) (on the line \(y=x\)). Solve \(x^{2}-4x+5=x\), then keep only solutions in the domain \(x\ge2\).

steps.explain: Intersections lie on \(y=x\): set \(f(x)=x\).
Quadratic formula.
Check the domain \(x\ge2\): \(\dfrac{5-\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx1.38<2\) (rejected); \(\dfrac{5+\sqrt{5}}{2}\approx3.62\ge2\) ✓.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5\). What is the equation of \(y=f^{-1}(x)\)?
questions.hint: Swap \(x\) and \(y\), then solve for \(y\) (complete the square first). Choose the sign of the square root that matches the range of the inverse: \(y\ge2\).

steps.explain: Write \(y=f(x)\) and swap \(x\) and \(y\).
Complete the square: \(y^{2}-4y+5=(y-2)^{2}+1\).
Take the square root (\(\pm\)).
The range of the inverse equals the domain of \(f\): \(y\ge2\). So we need the PLUS sign (\(2-\sqrt{x-1}\) is \(\le2\)).
Why not the others: B is the lower half (range \(y\le2\)); C is not a function (two values of \(y\)); D swaps the shifts.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Swap x and y; pick the sign using the range.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5\). For the restricted domain, sketch the function and the inverse function on the same number plane. Clearly label the graphs and show the main features. Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: The inverse is the REFLECTION of \(f\) in the line \(y=x\): swap the coordinates of every point. Plot \(f\) for \(x\ge2\) (vertex \((2,1)\)), then reflect.

steps.explain: Graph of \(f\) on the restricted domain \(x\ge2\): half a parabola starting at the vertex \((2,1)\) and rising steeply (blue).
Graph of \(f^{-1}\): swap coordinates. The vertex \((2,1)\) becomes \((1,2)\); it is the half of a sideways parabola \(y=2+\sqrt{x-1}\), starting at \((1,2)\) and rising slowly (green).
The two graphs meet on the line \(y=x\) (dashed) at \(\left(\dfrac{5+\sqrt{5}}{2},\dfrac{5+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\approx(3.62,3.62)\).

questions.stem: A function is defined as \(f(x)=x^{2}+2x-15\). The graphs of \(y=f(x)\) and of the line \(y=x\) are shown on the diagram. Determine the equation of the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\).
questions.hint: Take \(f\) on its restricted domain \(x\geq-1\) (from part i). Swap \(x\) and \(y\), complete the square to solve for \(y\), and choose the \(\pm\) using the range of the inverse \((y\geq-1)\).

steps.explain: Swap \(x\) and \(y\) (the domain and range of \(f\) swap).
Complete the square in \(y\): add \(16\) to both sides (\(y^{2}+2y+1=(y+1)^{2}\) and \(-15+1=-14\) wait: move \(-15\) first).
Add 1 to both sides to complete the square.
Take the square root of both sides; do not forget \(\pm\).

The inverse's range equals \(f\)'s domain \(x\geq-1\), so \(y\geq-1\): choose the PLUS sign (the minus sign would give \(y\leq-1\)). The blue curve starts at \((-16,-1)\) and stays at or above \(y=-1\).
Why not the others: B uses the wrong sign (\(y\leq-1\)); C has \(+1\); D has \(x-16\) (an arithmetic error when moving \(-15\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Swap \(x\) and \(y\), complete the square, choose \(\pm\) from the range \(y\geq-1\).

questions.stem: Find the inverse \(f^{-1}\) of \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-x}\).
questions.hint: Write \(y=f(x)\), SWAP \(x\) and \(y\), then solve for \(y\). To remove the square root, square both sides. The domain of the inverse is the RANGE of \(f\) (a square root is never negative, so \(x\geq0\)).

steps.explain: Write \(f(x)\) as \(y\).
Swap \(x\) and \(y\) (this is what an inverse does).
Square both sides to remove the root.
Solve for \(y\): add \(y\), subtract \(x^{2}\).
Domain of \(f^{-1}\) = range of \(f\). Since \(\sqrt{\ }\geq0\), \(f\) outputs only \(y\geq0\), so \(f^{-1}\) is only valid for \(x\geq0\) (otherwise \(x=\sqrt{4-y}\) could not be negative).
Check: \(f(0)=2\) so \(f^{-1}(2)\) must be 0: \(4-2^{2}=0\) ✓. Why not the others: B has the sign of \(x^{2}\) wrong; C adds; D squares \(4-x\) instead of \(x\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Swap \(x\) and \(y\), square both sides; domain \(x\geq0\).

questions.stem: Show that \(f(f^{-1}(x))=x\) and \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\). (Here \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-x}\) and \(f^{-1}(x)=4-x^{2},\ x\geq0\).) Which working is correct?
questions.hint: Composite: put the INSIDE function into every \(x\) of the OUTSIDE function. Simplify carefully: \(\left(\sqrt{A}\right)^{2}=A\), and \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=x\) when \(x\geq0\).

steps.explain: First composite \(f(f^{-1}(x))\): the inside is \(f^{-1}(x)=4-x^{2}\). Substitute it for \(x\) in \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-x}\).
Remove the brackets: \(4-(4-x^{2})=4-4+x^{2}=x^{2}\).
\(\sqrt{x^{2}}=|x|\), and the domain of \(f^{-1}\) is \(x\geq0\), so \(|x|=x\).
Second composite \(f^{-1}(f(x))\): the inside is \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-x}\). Put it in \(f^{-1}(x)=4-x^{2}\) (square it!).
A square root squared gives what is inside: \(\left(\sqrt{4-x}\right)^{2}=4-x\).
Both composites give \(x\), the mark of inverse functions.
Why not the others: B drops a bracket (\(4-4-x^{2}\)); C says \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=x^{2}\) and forgets to square the root; D mis-simplifies \(4-4+x\) as \(-x\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Substitute the inside function; \((\sqrt{A})^{2}=A\) and \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=x\) for \(x\geq0\).

questions.stem: Consider \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x\). Find the inverse of \(f(x)=x^{2}-4x,\ x\leq2\).
questions.hint: Swap \(x\) and \(y\), complete the square in \(y\), take the square root with \(\pm\), and use the range of the inverse (\(y\leq2\)) to pick the MINUS sign.

steps.explain: Write \(y=x^{2}-4x\) and swap \(x\) and \(y\).
Complete the square: add \(4\) to both sides (half of \(-4\) is \(-2\), squared is 4).
Take the square root of both sides with \(\pm\).
The range of \(f^{-1}\) is \(y\leq2\) (part iii), so choose the MINUS sign (it gives values \(\leq2\)).
Check: \(f(0)=0\) so \(f^{-1}(0)\) must be 0: \(2-\sqrt{4}=0\) ✓. Why not the others: B uses the plus sign (range \(y\geq2\), the inverse of the OTHER half); C has \(-2\); D has \(x-4\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Swap, complete the square, minus sign because \(y\leq2\).

questions.stem: \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\) is monotonic with domain \(0\le x\le16\) and range \(0\le y\le2\), so an inverse function exists. Find the domain and range of \(f^{-1}(x)\). Hence find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
questions.hint: The inverse SWAPS domain and range. To find the formula: write \(y=f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), and solve for \(y\). Square twice to remove both roots, and remember \(4-\sqrt{y}\ge0\) must hold.

steps.explain: Domain and range swap: \(\mathrm{dom}(f^{-1})=\mathrm{ran}(f)=[0,2]\) and \(\mathrm{ran}(f^{-1})=\mathrm{dom}(f)=[0,16]\).
Swap \(x\) and \(y\) in \(y=\sqrt{4-\sqrt{x}}\): \(x=\sqrt{4-\sqrt{y}}\).
Square both sides to remove the outer root: \(x^{2}=4-\sqrt{y}\). Then \(\sqrt{y}=4-x^{2}\).
Square again: \(y=\left(4-x^{2}\right)^{2}\). On the domain \(0\le x\le2\) we have \(4-x^{2}\ge0\), consistent with \(\sqrt{y}\ge0\).

Check: \(f^{-1}(0)=16\) and \(f^{-1}(2)=0\), matching the reflected points \((16,0)\to(0,16)\) and \((0,2)\to(2,0)\) ✓. Why not the others: B keeps the old domain; C only squares once (\(4-x^{4}\) is wrong); D is \(f\) itself (not the inverse).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the domain and range of \(f^{-1}(x)\). Hence find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
keyPoints.note: Swap \(x,y\); square twice; domain/range swap.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=e^{-x}-2x\). Explain why the inverse of \(f(x)\) is a function.
options: \(f'(x)=-e^{-x}-2<0\) for all \(x\), so \(f\) is strictly decreasing, hence one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test), so its inverse is a function.
\(f'(x)=-e^{-x}-2\) is never zero, so the graph has no turning points; therefore the inverse is a function (an increasing function is required).
\(f(0)=1\) and \(f(1)<f(0)\), so \(f\) is decreasing; one example shows the inverse is a function.
\(f(x)\) is defined for all real \(x\), so its inverse is a function.
questions.hint: The inverse of \(f\) is a FUNCTION exactly when \(f\) is ONE-TO-ONE (each \(y\) comes from only one \(x\): the horizontal line test). A function that is always decreasing (or always increasing) is one-to-one. Show \(f'(x)<0\) for all \(x\).

steps.explain: Differentiate: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x}\) and \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(-2x)=-2\).
Sign: \(e^{-x}>0\) for all \(x\), so \(-e^{-x}<0\), and \(-2<0\). The sum of two negatives is negative.
A function with \(f'(x)<0\) everywhere is strictly DECREASING, so it never takes the same value twice: it is one-to-one (any horizontal line cuts the graph at most once).

Why not the others: B says an increasing function is required (a decreasing one is fine too) and “never zero” alone is not enough; C uses one example (not a proof); D: being defined everywhere does not make a function one-to-one (e.g. \(x^{2}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Explain why the inverse of \(f(x)\) is a function.
keyPoints.note: \(f\,'<0\) always \(\Rightarrow\) one-to-one \(\Rightarrow\) inverse function.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=e^{-x}-2x\) and \(g(x)=f^{-1}(x)\). Find the gradient of \(g(x)\) where its graph cuts the \(x\)-axis.
questions.hint: Gradient of the inverse: \(g'(a)=\dfrac{1}{f'(g(a))}\). The graph of \(g\) cuts the \(x\)-axis where \(g(x)=0\); since \(g=f^{-1}\), \(g(x)=0\Leftrightarrow x=f(0)\). Find that \(x\), then evaluate \(f'(0)\).

steps.explain: Gradient of an inverse function: the reciprocal of the gradient of \(f\) at the corresponding point (reflection in \(y=x\) swaps \(x\) and \(y\)). \(g'(1)=\dfrac{1}{f'(g(1))}=\dfrac{1}{f'(0)}\).
Reciprocal.
Why not the others: B (\(-3\)) is \(f'(0)\) itself (not the reciprocal); C has the wrong sign (an inverse of a decreasing function is also decreasing); D uses \(f'(0)=-2\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.hint: Eliminate the parameter \(t\): make \(t\) the subject of the simple equation \(x=2t-5\), then substitute into \(y\).

steps.explain: Use the equation with the simpler \(t\): \(x=2t-5\). Add 5 then divide by 2 to make \(t\) the subject.
Substitute this into \(y=12t^{2}+1\). Put the whole expression in a bracket before squaring.
Square the bracket: \(\left(\dfrac{x+5}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{(x+5)^{2}}{4}\), and \(12\div 4=3\).

So the correct choice is option A.

questions.hint: Each piece is continuous by itself. The only place a join can fail is \(x=1\). Continuity there means the two pieces give the SAME value at \(x=1\): \(\lim_{x\to1^{-}}f=f(1)\).

Factorise.

Substitute into \(y=4\cos t-1\) in the same way.
The point is on the circle at \(45^{\circ}\) from the vertical (green radius). Its horizontal distance from the centre is \(4\sin t=2\sqrt{2}\) and vertical distance \(4\cos t=2\sqrt{2}\) (purple).

questions.stem: A curve is represented by the following parametric equations \(x=2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta\), \(y=2\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\). Find the cartesian equation of the curve.
questions.hint: Add and subtract the two equations to isolate \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) separately, then use \(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1\).

steps.explain: ADD the equations: the \(\cos\theta\) terms cancel.
SUBTRACT (first minus second): the \(\sin\theta\) terms cancel.
Use the Pythagorean identity.
Multiply by the common denominator 144.
Check with \(\theta=0\): \((x,y)=(3,-3)\): \(13(9)+13(9)+10(-9)=117+117-90=144\) ✓. Why not the others: B has the wrong sign on \(xy\); C and D forget the cross-term.
So the correct choice is option A.
